paragraphs: Four explosions tore through Krakatoa on the morning of 27 August 1883, the loudest at 10:02 a.m. registering as the loudest sound ever recorded by human ears, heard in Perth, nearly 2,000 miles away, and on Rodrigues Island, 3,000 miles out in the Indian Ocean. More than two thirds of the island collapsed into the caldera the blast tore open beneath it.

Most of the roughly 36,000 dead drowned, pushed under by waves the collapse threw up, some reaching 41 metres, that swept the coasts of Java and Sumatra. A smaller share, put at around a tenth, were killed onshore by pyroclastic flows that crossed open water and burned fishing villages. A new cone, Anak Krakatau, broke the surface of the same caldera in the late 1920s and still erupts.

The only account comes from Gabriele de Mussis, a notary in Piacenza who never set foot in Caffa himself. Writing around 1348 from stories told by returning merchants, he says the Mongols flung their own plague dead over the walls in early 1346, hoping panic and the stench would break the siege.

Most historians now doubt the corpses did much of the work. Plague travels in fleas riding on rats, not in flung bodies, and Genoese ships kept crossing the Black Sea regardless of the fighting. That traffic carried the disease to Constantinople by 1347 and to Messina, Sicily, that October, aboard twelve galleys already crewed by the dying.
